name: Adam Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play small percussion parts for a theatre, record short sound cues and assist a qualified tutor with adult rhythm lessons. I used to manage a food shop and took up paid music five years ago. I finished secondary school, and I still ask the sound lead to check a difficult entrance.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What have you built outside the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner and I have grown children and a mortgage. We saved eleven months of expenses from years at the shop and our present work pays well, though I have not asked for a written retirement estimate yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that a quicker cue sheet, the list of sound moments, is useful if the paid call stays on it. I would keep playing for the live show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eleven months saved and several nearby theatres give us room if one cue order goes. My partner’s wages and my regular shows cover the mortgage now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This season I would keep paid percussion calls, cue recordings and four supervised adult pupils. I use AI occasionally to sort rehearsal notes, but I play every rhythm before handing it to the tutor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel calm. A little booking software does not change what I earn this term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you verify a new theatre date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the sound lead for a written call sheet with fee and finish time. I will not hold an evening for a spoken maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about retirement income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request a written estimate this winter while keeping the shows. I do not yet know what it will say.

Request **written call fees** and finish times before extra dates.

feel: I feel **calm** about secure current work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre manager that software may write a sound cue cheaply, but an actor still needs a musician to follow the stage. I would ask which recording and rehearsal hours remain paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cues are about a third of my own pay, and a generator could take those orders. The live shows are booked, but I cannot assume they replace every lost session.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would ask for a written quarter of paid theatre calls and a paid sound-lead lesson on the new timing checker. In the first year I would test only a percussion take I own without actor or pupil names if studio storage is approved locally; I would compare each beat by ear with the original and stop if timing changes or a file leaves the theatre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about cue fees. Savings give me a search window, not a replacement booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you feed a pupil’s recording into the checker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A pupil’s name and voice stay in the lesson folder; a nameless take I own is enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try a different theatre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if paid cue hours actually fall. I would apply for a posted paid percussion-assistant seat if my secondary schooling and supervised experience qualify, written net pay after travel replaces lost sessions and the last bus runs; I would keep current calls until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that AGI by 2028 could make an entire cue before the cast rehearses. I want signed paid calls for the percussionists who still play in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the small cue orders to end in 2028, and the theatre might cut some live rehearsals as well. Playing robots follow about three years later, around 2031. Recording fees can end before any robot lifts a drum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would total cue invoices and ask for signed paid rehearsal dates. In the first year after 2028, if paid percussion calls also fall, I would apply for a posted adult-music assistant job only if my schooling and supervised teaching qualify, written net pay after travel replaces lost calls and the bus gets me home; I would keep current theatre and pupil hours until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing cue work and perhaps some rehearsals. Eleven months saved and several local openings give me time to choose without missing the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a costly microphone now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a signed paid recording order covers its cost. I would keep eight months of household expenses untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you stop work at 60 instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 60 in 2028, but I have no written retirement figure. I would request one and keep paid work while I check it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre manager that five years until AGI by 2031 is time to train sound assistants while there are still live shows. Training hours should be paid, just like rehearsals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cues may stop selling by 2031 and playing robots may arrive around 2034. A sound job could replace those fees if I qualify, but a course without a wage is not a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would take a six-month live-sound certificate only if the theatre offers a real funded place, paid training hours and a schedule that fits the last bus without reducing my partner’s paid shifts. In the first year after 2031, if cue or rehearsal fees fall, I would apply for a posted paid sound-assistant role only if the certificate qualifies me, written net pay after travel replaces the lost fees and the bus still runs; I would keep theatre and supervised pupil work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until the course points to a real paid seat. I will not spend the mortgage reserve on an unpaid certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run a crowded show alone after the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The house sound lead must supervise my first checks. I would not operate a crowded night alone until equipment and safety checks are signed off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if tuition is funded but the hours are unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid theatre calls and ask for a paid intake. Free sound-course tuition cannot replace the wages I lose to attend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that ten years until AGI by 2036 lets us set written pay for preparation and training. I would also ask the musicians’ association to bring the fee sheets, not just speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cue fees may end by 2036 and robots might play drums around 2039. We have eleven months saved and nearby theatres today, but I have not yet seen a retirement statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year I would request a written retirement estimate and ask the association for a two-year paid rehearsal agreement. I would save ten percent of each extra paid event call after mortgage, food and travel, aiming for fifteen months while leaving eight untouched; in the first year after 2036, if cue and paid show hours fall, I would apply for a posted theatre music aide role only if my schooling qualifies, written net pay after travel covers the lost fees and the last bus runs, keeping current work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about that distant risk because work and savings hold now. A decade is useful only if I get real paid terms in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra event call pays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I save nothing new that week. Eight months of expenses stay untouched rather than become a speculative tuition fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you promise to stop at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 68 in 2036, but no pension figure has been checked. I would decide only after seeing the written estimate and current paid work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because cue orders could stop before I know which rehearsals the theatre still pays. Signed dates, an actual posted aide role and the bus home would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs off the first safety check. A junior musician should not be handed a crowded show and a shrug.

headlineQuote: A junior musician should not be handed a crowded show and a shrug.
portrait: At **58**, Adam is a junior percussionist who came from food retail and completed secondary school.
His higher **musician pay**, eleven-month reserve and nearby theatres give room to search after a lost cue order.
He uses **AI occasionally**, testing a new checker only after paid instruction, local storage approval and ear comparison.
A **funded sound course** needs paid hours and bus access before qualified posted sound work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase cue orders before the theatre confirms its paid rehearsals.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed theatre dates**, a qualified posted aide opening with written net pay and the last bus home would help Adam.
